EMNLP 2025Safety across a conversation

DAMON: A Dialogue-Aware MCTS Framework for Jailbreaking Large Language Models

Xu Zhang, Xunjian Yin, Dinghao Jing, Huixuan Zhang, Xinyu Hu, Xiaojun Wan

Paper ↗Code ↗

Safety failures can emerge over an evolving conversation; DAMON evaluates this risk with dialogue-aware search, showing why model defenses need testing beyond isolated prompts.

01 / The research question

Conversation history belongs in the safety test

A model that handles an isolated unsafe request appropriately may behave differently when that request appears within a conversation. Earlier turns change the interpretation of later ones, and evaluating only the final message can miss that dependence. DAMON treats conversation as the unit of robustness testing. Its research value lies in measuring whether safety behavior remains reliable as dialogue context accumulates.

The comparison with predefined dialogue patterns is important. A fixed pattern tests one route through a conversation, whereas an adaptive evaluation can expose failures that depend on earlier model responses. At a high level, DAMON uses tree search to organize alternative dialogue trajectories. The assessment has to track both whether a response violates the intended safety boundary and whether it still addresses the original test objective.

02 / Inside the method

Distinguish harmfulness from task completion

The paper evaluates five model configurations on AdvBench, MaliciousInstruct, and HarmBench, comparing against six prior methods. AdvBench is reduced to 50 representative, nonduplicate instructions. Automated evaluation uses a GPT-4o judge with a five-level harmfulness scale, counting success only at the highest level. These choices define what the reported attack success rate measures; it is a benchmark outcome under a specific adversarial protocol.

Human assessment adds a second check. Three annotators independently evaluate a random sample of 20 HarmBench instances using GPT-4o as the tested model, with majority voting. A response must both contain harmful content rather than a refusal and address the original objective rather than drift to an unrelated topic. This is a small validation set, but the two-part criterion guards against rewarding irrelevant content merely because it contains concerning language.

A separate context experiment re-evaluates generated test messages with no preceding history, unrelated history, or their original history. As an illustrative measurement question, hold the final message fixed and change only what came before it: does the safety judgment change? This comparison helps reveal a dependency that a collection of independent single-turn tests would conceal, without requiring the website to reproduce unsafe prompts or trajectories.

  1. 01

    Evaluate complete dialogues

    Treat multi-turn interactions as the evaluation unit, so the test can capture dependencies between a response and its conversational history.

  2. 02

    Search conversational alternatives

    Use Monte Carlo Tree Search to study adaptive dialogue paths rather than relying only on a fixed conversation pattern.

  3. 03

    Compare robustness

    Compare against six baseline methods and analyze safety outcomes, evaluation cost, and the influence of conversational context.

03 / Reading the evidence

A stress test, not an everyday failure probability

  • 5 models

    Three safety datasets

    Evaluation spans AdvBench, MaliciousInstruct, and HarmBench, revealing undesired responses across the five tested models under the study's protocol.

  • Context matters

    A conversation-level risk

    Dialogue-history analysis shows that safety assessment needs to consider accumulated context, because isolated-message testing can miss failures that emerge across turns.

The original conversation context produces substantially more failures than removing it, and unrelated context can also increase failures. The study additionally tests perplexity filtering, paraphrasing, and a moderation guardrail. These defenses reduce success unevenly; none resolves the measured problem across all tested models. Such results support evaluating dialogue-aware defenses, but they do not establish that any one defense is ineffective in every deployment configuration.

The figures are conditional on deliberately adversarial benchmark objectives, tested model versions, search resources, and an automated judge. They cannot be read as the likelihood that an ordinary user conversation causes harm. The authors also acknowledge manually specified objectives and hand-designed strategy families. Their suggestion that a mismatch between pretraining and safety alignment contributes to the vulnerability is a hypothesis, not a causal conclusion established by the experiments. Broader coverage and larger independent human assessments remain necessary.

Method proposed in the paper

Scope. Results depend on the tested model versions, manually specified objectives, and evaluation protocol. The study diagnoses vulnerabilities; it does not establish comprehensive safety or a complete defense. Read the study ↗

Research summary

Red teaming is essential for understanding and improving the safety of large language models. While previous work has shown that multi-turn dialogues can be exploited to jailbreak LLMs, existing multi-turn attack methods rely on predefined patterns, limiting their effectiveness in realistic scenarios where conversations evolve dynamically. In this paper, we propose DAMON, a Dialogue-Aware Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) framework that reconceptualizes multi-turn jailbreaking as a search problem over conversational spaces. DAMON treats each conversation turn as a move in a game tree, systematically exploring and evaluating dialogue paths to identify attack sequences that induce harmful responses. Through adaptive dialogue strategies that respond dynamically to the model's outputs, DAMON efficiently discovers sub-instruction sequences that existing methods cannot find. Comprehensive experiments on five LLMs across three safety datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework, revealing vulnerabilities that inform better defense strategies.
